items.title: An upper sum for a line
items.prose: Take $f(x) = x$ on $[0, 2]$ with $n = 8$ equal pieces of width $\tfrac14$.
items.question: What is the upper sum $U$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the right ends $\tfrac14, \tfrac24, \dots, 2$ and multiply by $\tfrac14$.

byKey.left: You used the left ends, giving the lower sum $\tfrac74$.
byKey.no-width: You added the eight tops, 9, but did not multiply by the width $\tfrac14$.

explain.text: The right ends $\tfrac k4$ for $k = 1$ to 8 add to $\tfrac{36}{4} = 9$. Times the width $\tfrac14$ gives $U = \tfrac94 = 2.25$. The lower sum is $\tfrac74 = 1.75$, and the integral 2 lies between.

items.title: The gap for a line, in general
items.prose: For $f(x) = x$ on $[0, 2]$ with $n$ equal pieces, $U_n = \tfrac2n \sum_{k=1}^{n} \tfrac{2k}{n}$ and $L_n = \tfrac2n \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \tfrac{2k}{n}$. At $n = 8$ the gap is $\tfrac94 - \tfrac74 = \tfrac12$.
items.question: Give $U_n - L_n$ as a formula in $n$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The sums differ only in their first and last terms.

byKey.two: You kept the width $\tfrac2n$ but dropped the rise 2. The gap is rise times width: $2 \times \tfrac2n$.
byKey.one: That was the gap for $x^2$ on $[0, 1]$. Here the rise is 2 and the width $\tfrac2n$.
byKey.sq: You divided by $n$ once too often. The telescoped heights add to 2, a fixed number.

explain.text: The two sums share every term except $\tfrac{2n}{n} = 2$ in $U_n$ and $0$ in $L_n$. So $U_n - L_n = \tfrac2n \times 2 = \tfrac4n$, which is $\tfrac12$ at $n = 8$. It tends to 0, so $x$ is integrable on $[0, 2]$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Differentiate each part with part one, using the chain rule on $x^2$.

byKey.upper: You differentiated only the upper part, $\tfrac{2x}{x^2} = \tfrac2x$. The lower limit subtracts $\tfrac1x$.
byKey.nochain: You read $\tfrac1t$ at $x^2$ but forgot the factor $2x$.
byKey.sign: You added the lower limit's term. Raising the lower limit removes area: subtract.

explain.text: Part one and the chain rule give $\tfrac{1}{x^2} \cdot 2x - \tfrac1x = \tfrac1x$. As a check, $G(x) = \ln(x^2) - \ln x = \ln x$. Both limits move, so both contribute.

items.title: Closed subsets of compact sets
items.prose: Prove: if $K$ is compact and $F \subseteq K$ is closed, then $F$ is compact. One line is flawed.
items.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Each $x_n$ is in $K$, so compactness of $K$ gives a subsequence $x_{n_k} \to x$ with $x \in K$.
The terms $x_{n_k}$ lie in $F$ and $F$ is closed, so the limit $x$ lies in $F$ (l23).
So every sequence in $F$ has a subsequence converging in $F$: $F$ is compact. $\blacksquare$
$F$ is bounded, so Bolzano-Weierstrass gives a convergent subsequence.
lines.why: In a general metric space, bounded gives no subsequence. Compactness of $K$ supplies it.

feedback.correct: Right. $K$ gives the subsequence, closedness of $F$ keeps the limit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take a sequence, use $K$ for a subsequence, then $F$ closed for the limit.

byKey.d1: You used Bolzano-Weierstrass. In a metric space, compactness of $K$ is what gives the subsequence.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: Compactness of $K$ finds a convergent subsequence with limit in $K$. Closedness of $F$ moves the limit into $F$. This is why closed, bounded sets in $\mathbb{R}$ are compact: they are closed subsets of some $[a, b]$.

items.title: Continuous images of compact sets
items.prose: Prove: if $f: K \to Y$ is continuous between metric spaces and $K$ is compact, then $f(K)$ is compact. Continuity gives $f(x_n) \to f(x)$ whenever $x_n \to x$ in $K$. One line is flawed.
items.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Compactness of $K$ gives a subsequence $x_{n_k} \to x \in K$.
By continuity, $y_{n_k} = f(x_{n_k}) \to f(x)$, and $f(x) \in f(K)$. So $f(K)$ is compact. $\blacksquare$
Since $f(K)$ is closed, the limit of $(y_n)$ lies in $f(K)$.
lines.why: We do not know yet that $f(K)$ is closed, nor that $(y_n)$ converges. Both come out of the proof.

feedback.correct: Right. Pull back to $K$, extract, push forward by continuity.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Lift each $y_n$ to some $x_n \in K$ first.

byKey.d1: You assumed $f(K)$ closed and $(y_n)$ convergent. Neither is known.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: Each $y_n$ comes from some $x_n$ in $K$, where compactness acts, and continuity carries the convergent subsequence across. With $Y = \mathbb{R}$ and $K$ nonempty this gives the extreme value theorem again. The set $f(K)$ is closed and bounded, so it holds its sup.

items.title: One delta on a longer interval
items.question: What $\delta$ does this bound give for $\varepsilon = 0.03$?

byKey.half: You divided by 2, as on $[0, 1]$. On $[0, 3]$ the factor $|x + y|$ reaches 6.
byKey.times: You multiplied by 6. The window must shrink: divide.

explain.text: $|x - y| < 0.005$ gives $|x^2 - y^2| \le 6|x - y| < 0.03$. The factor 6 is the largest $|x + y|$ on $[0, 3]$. On a longer interval the factor grows, which is why no single $\delta$ works on all of $\mathbb{R}$.

items.title: Which formulas are metrics
items.prose: Each formula defines $d(x, y)$ for real $x$ and $y$.
items.question: Select all that apply: which are metrics on $\mathbb{R}$?

options.why: At 0, 1, 2: $4 > 1 + 1$, so the triangle inequality fails.

feedback.correct: Right. The capped distance and $|x^3 - y^3|$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each formula against all three axioms, with a counterexample where one fails.

byKey.sq: You accepted $|x - y|^2$. Squaring breaks the triangle inequality at 0, 1, 2.
byKey.sin: You accepted $|\sin x - \sin y|$. Different points can share a sine.
byKey.half: You accepted $|x - 2y|$. It is not even zero at $x = y = 1$.

explain.text: $|x^3 - y^3|$ is $|u - v|$ for $u = x^3$, and cubing is one to one, so it is a metric. For the cap, $\min(1, a + b) \le \min(1, a) + \min(1, b)$ gives the triangle inequality. The other three each break one axiom.

items.title: Upper and lower sums for a function that turns
items.prose: Write `upper_lower_turns(f, a, b, n, turns)`. Here $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$. It is monotone between consecutive points of the sorted list `turns`, its turning points. Return $(U, L)$ for $n$ equal pieces, exactly for `Fraction` inputs.

params.title: Expected
lines: >>> upper_lower_turns(lambda x: x * (1 - x), Fraction(0), Fraction(1), 3, [Fraction(1, 2)])

items.question: Complete the function.

widget.starter:

def upper_lower_turns(f, a, b, n, turns):

    monotone between consecutive points of turns."""
    ...
widget.solution:
from fractions import Fraction

def upper_lower_turns(f, a, b, n, turns):
    """(U, L) on [a, b] with n equal pieces. f is continuous and
    monotone between consecutive points of turns."""
    w = (b - a) / n
    U = L = 0
    for k in range(n):
        lo, hi = a + k * w, a + (k + 1) * w
        # the sup and inf sit at an end or at a turn inside
        vals = [f(lo), f(hi)] + [f(t) for t in turns if lo < t < hi]
        U += max(vals) * w
        L += min(vals) * w
    return (U, L)

examples.call: upper_lower_turns(lambda x: x * (1 - x), Fraction(0), Fraction(1), 3, [Fraction(1, 2)])

tests.call: upper_lower_turns(lambda x: x * (1 - x), Fraction(0), Fraction(1), 4, [Fraction(1, 2)])
upper_lower_turns(lambda x: x * (1 - x), Fraction(0), Fraction(1), 3, [Fraction(1, 2)])
upper_lower_turns(lambda x: x * x, Fraction(-1), Fraction(1), 2, [Fraction(0)])
upper_lower_turns(lambda x: x * x, Fraction(-1), Fraction(1), 3, [Fraction(0)])
upper_lower_turns(lambda x: x**3 - 3 * x, Fraction(-2), Fraction(2), 4, [Fraction(-1), Fraction(1)])
upper_lower_turns(lambda x: x**3 - 3 * x, Fraction(-2), Fraction(2), 3, [Fraction(-1), Fraction(1)])

isinstance(upper_lower_turns(lambda x: x * x, Fraction(-1), Fraction(1), 3, [Fraction(0)])[1], Fraction)

widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests, compared exactly. Two use x(1 - x) on [0, 1], with 3 and 4 pieces. Two use x^2 on [-1, 1], with 2 and 3 pieces. Two use x^3 - 3x on [-2, 2], turning at -1 and 1. Two are monotone with no turns, and one checks for a Fraction result.

feedback.correct: Right. On each piece the sup and inf are at an end or at a turn inside.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. On each piece compare $f$ at both ends and at every turning point strictly inside.

explain.text: Between turns $f$ is monotone, so on a piece its extremes are among the end values and the turns inside. For $x(1 - x)$ with three pieces, the middle piece holds the turn $\tfrac12$, so its top is $\tfrac14$, not $\tfrac29$. That gives $U = \tfrac{25}{108}$ and $L = \tfrac{2}{27}$.

items.title: A proof that proves too much
items.prose: Claim: $(0, 1)$ is compact. Proof: (1) Let $(x_n)$ be a sequence in $(0, 1)$. (2) It is bounded. (3) By Bolzano-Weierstrass a subsequence $x_{n_k}$ converges, to $x$ say. (4) So $(0, 1)$ is compact.
items.question: Which line is flawed?

options.text: Line 4: the limit $x$ may be 0 or 1, outside $(0, 1)$, so the conclusion does not follow.
Line 2: a sequence in $(0, 1)$ need not be bounded.
options.why: Every term lies between 0 and 1, so it is bounded.

options.text: Line 3: Bolzano-Weierstrass needs a closed interval.
options.why: Bolzano-Weierstrass needs only a bounded sequence. It gives a limit, just not its location.

options.text: Line 1: we must take every sequence, not one.
options.why: $(x_n)$ is arbitrary, which is exactly 'every sequence'.

feedback.correct: Right. Compactness needs the limit inside the set.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the conclusion with the definition: where must the limit lie?

explain.text: Compact asks for a subsequence converging to a point of the set. Line 3 gives a limit in $[0, 1]$ only, and $\tfrac1n$ shows it can be 0. The proof never used closedness, which $(0, 1)$ lacks.

items.title: Continuous functions are Riemann integrable
items.prompt:
Let $f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous.

(a) Prove that $f$ is uniformly continuous on $[a, b]$. You may use Bolzano-Weierstrass.

(b) Deduce that $f$ is Riemann integrable: for every $\varepsilon > 0$, find a partition $P$ with $U(f, P) - L(f, P) < \varepsilon$. You may use the extreme value theorem.

(c) Optional, one more point: for $f(x) = x^2$ on $[0, 1]$ and $\varepsilon = 0.01$, how many equal pieces does your argument ask for? Compare with the exact gap $U_n - L_n = \tfrac1n$.

Give a reason for every line.
items.model:
**(a) Uniform continuity.** Suppose not. Then some $\varepsilon_0 > 0$ has no working $\delta$. Taking $\delta = \tfrac1n$, there are $x_n, y_n \in [a, b]$ with $|x_n - y_n| < \tfrac1n$ and $|f(x_n) - f(y_n)| \ge \varepsilon_0$.

$(x_n)$ is bounded, so by Bolzano-Weierstrass a subsequence $x_{n_k} \to c$. Since $a \le x_{n_k} \le b$ and limits keep $\le$, $c \in [a, b]$.

$|y_{n_k} - c| \le |y_{n_k} - x_{n_k}| + |x_{n_k} - c| < \tfrac1{n_k} + |x_{n_k} - c| \to 0$, so $y_{n_k} \to c$ too.

$f$ is continuous at $c$, so $f(x_{n_k}) \to f(c)$ and $f(y_{n_k}) \to f(c)$. Hence $|f(x_{n_k}) - f(y_{n_k})| \to 0$, contradicting $|f(x_{n_k}) - f(y_{n_k})| \ge \varepsilon_0$ for all $k$. $\blacksquare$

**(b) Integrability.** Let $\varepsilon > 0$. By (a) choose $\delta > 0$ with $|x - y| < \delta \Rightarrow |f(x) - f(y)| < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{b - a}$. Let $P$ be any partition whose pieces all have width less than $\delta$. Equal pieces with $\tfrac{b - a}{n} < \delta$ will do, by Archimedes.

On each piece $[x_{k-1}, x_k]$, $f$ is continuous. By the extreme value theorem it attains $M_k = f(s_k)$ and $m_k = f(t_k)$, with $s_k, t_k$ in the piece. Then $|s_k - t_k| < \delta$, so $M_k - m_k < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{b - a}$.

So $U(f, P) - L(f, P) = \sum_k (M_k - m_k)\,\Delta x_k < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{b - a}\sum_k \Delta x_k = \varepsilon$. By the criterion, $f$ is integrable. $\blacksquare$

**(c)** Here $b - a = 1$, so we need $|x^2 - y^2| < 0.01$. Since $|x^2 - y^2| = |x - y|\,|x + y| \le 2|x - y|$ on $[0, 1]$, $\delta = 0.005$ works. Equal pieces need $\tfrac1n < 0.005$, so $n > 200$: $n = 201$. The exact gap $\tfrac1n < 0.01$ needs only $n = 101$. The proof's bound is about twice as many pieces as needed; it is safe, not sharp.

rubric.text: (a) Negates uniform continuity correctly: one $\varepsilon_0$, and pairs $x_n, y_n$ with $|x_n - y_n| < \tfrac1n$ and $|f(x_n) - f(y_n)| \ge \varepsilon_0$.
(a) Extracts $x_{n_k} \to c$ by Bolzano-Weierstrass and shows $c \in [a, b]$ using closedness.
(a) Shows $y_{n_k} \to c$ by the triangle inequality.
(a) Uses continuity at $c$ to reach the contradiction.
(b) Chooses one $\delta$ for the tolerance $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{b - a}$, independent of the point.
(b) Takes a mesh below $\delta$ and bounds each $M_k - m_k$, citing the extreme value theorem.
(b) Sums $(M_k - m_k)\,\Delta x_k$ to get $U - L < \varepsilon$.
(c) Gives $\delta = 0.005$, $n = 201$, and compares with the exact $n = 101$.
